title: Numbers you must know cold
intro: Estimation in an interview is not about precision; it is about speed and orders of magnitude. These anchors let you derive any number in under a minute. Memorize them, then practice the recipes until the arithmetic is boring.

recipes.name: Requests per second from daily users
steps: DAU times actions per user per day gives requests per day.
Divide by 100K (seconds in a day, rounded) for average RPS.
Multiply by the peak factor: 3 to 5 for consumer, 5 to 10 for B2B, up to 100 for seasonal retail.
recipes.example: 50M DAU, 10 actions each: 500M per day, 5K RPS average, 25K RPS at peak for a consumer app.

recipes.name: Storage from write rate
steps: Writes per day times bytes per record gives bytes per day.
Multiply by 365 for a year, then by retention years.
Add 50 to 100 percent for indexes and replication; multiply by replica count for total footprint.
recipes.example: 10M writes per day at 1 KB: 10 GB per day, 3.65 TB per year, about 7 TB with indexes, 21 TB across three replicas.

recipes.name: Bandwidth from traffic
steps: RPS times average response size gives bytes per second.
Multiply by 8 for bits; compare against NIC and CDN capacity.
Multiply by seconds per month for egress cost at about $0.08 per GB.
recipes.example: 20K RPS at 50 KB: 1 GB/s or 8 Gbps; about 2.6 PB per month, which is why a CDN pays for itself.

recipes.name: Cache size from working set
steps: Estimate the fraction of data read repeatedly (often 20 percent of keys take 80 percent of reads).
Multiply hot keys by value size for memory needed.
Target a hit rate; if the working set exceeds node memory, cluster or add a local L1.
recipes.example: 100M users, 20 percent active daily, 2 KB profile each: 40 GB of hot profiles, which fits one Redis node with headroom.

recipes.name: Shard count from write rate and size
steps: Take peak writes per second divided by what one primary comfortably sustains (say 10K).
Take total data divided by comfortable size per shard (say 1 to 2 TB).
Use the larger of the two, round up to a power of two, and allocate 4 to 8x that many logical shards for future moves.
recipes.example: 80K peak writes per second and 12 TB: 8 shards by writes, 8 by size; run 8 physical nodes with 64 logical shards.

recipes.name: Servers from throughput
steps: Peak RPS divided by RPS per instance (measured, or 1K to 5K for a typical service with a DB call).
Divide by target utilization (0.6 to 0.7) for headroom.
Add one more per availability zone so losing a zone keeps capacity.
recipes.example: 30K peak RPS at 2K per instance: 15 instances, 22 at 70 percent utilization, 25 across three zones.

recipes.name: Availability of a design
steps: List the components a request touches in series and multiply their availabilities.
For redundant pairs, compute 1 minus (failure rate squared) and use that in the series.
Compare with the SLO and name the weakest component.
recipes.example: Gateway 99.99, service 99.95, database 99.95, third-party 99.9: product is about 99.79 percent, and the third party is the cap.

drill.q: Round trip within a datacenter?
drill.a: About 0.5 ms. That is the price of one service hop before any work is done.

drill.q: Round trip New York to London?
drill.a: 70 to 80 ms. About 5 ms per 1,000 km of fiber each way, doubled, plus routing overhead.

drill.q: Redis GET including the network, same AZ?
Postgres indexed point read, warm cache?
drill.a: 1 to 5 ms, and about 10x worse on a disk read.

drill.q: Seconds in a day, and the shortcut?
drill.a: 86,400; call it 100K. So 1M requests per day is about 12 RPS.

drill.q: Writes per second one Postgres primary comfortably sustains?
drill.a: 5K to 20K TPS depending on instance and durability settings.

drill.q: Ops per second for one Redis node?
drill.a: 100K to 1M.

drill.q: 99.9 percent availability in downtime per month?
drill.a: About 43 minutes.

drill.q: 99.99 percent availability in downtime per month?
drill.a: About 4.4 minutes, which is beyond what humans can achieve manually.

drill.q: Three serial dependencies at 99.9 percent: composed availability?
drill.a: About 99.7 percent.

drill.q: Hot object storage price per GB-month?
drill.a: About $0.023; 1 TB is about $23 per month.

drill.q: Internet egress price per GB?
drill.a: About $0.05 to $0.09; 100 TB per month is $5K to $9K.

drill.q: Cross-AZ transfer price?
drill.a: About $0.01 per GB in each direction; the invisible line item.

drill.q: Spot discount range?
drill.a: 60 to 90 percent, with interruption.

drill.q: A minute of 1080p video?
drill.a: 50 to 100 MB stored; about 40 MB streamed at 5 Mbps.

drill.q: WebSocket connections per node?
drill.a: 100K to 1M, bounded by memory per connection.

drill.q: Peak-to-average factor for B2B SaaS?
drill.a: 5 to 10x, driven by the Monday 9am workday peak.

drill.q: Peak-to-average factor for seasonal e-commerce?
drill.a: 50 to 100x on Black Friday.

drill.q: How many values in a 64-bit id space?
drill.a: About 1.8 x 10^19.

drill.q: TLS 1.3 handshake round trips?
drill.a: One. TLS 1.2 is two. QUIC resumption can be zero.

drill.q: S3 request rate per prefix?
drill.a: 3,500 PUTs and 5,500 GETs per second, and it scales with more prefixes.

drill.q: Kafka throughput per broker?
drill.a: Hundreds of MB/s to about 1 GB/s; hundreds of thousands of small messages per second.

drill.q: Lambda cold start range?
drill.a: 100 ms to 2 s depending on runtime and package size.

drill.q: Latency a human perceives as instant?
drill.a: Under 100 ms. Under 1 s keeps flow; over 10 s loses attention.
